result: Family history of Alzheimer's disease (FH) was associated with lower PAL performance in individuals under 65 years old, with the effect diminishing after age 65 as indicated by the Age x FH interaction where trend lines cross at age 65.
evaluation: Reviewers acknowledge this as the 'most significant finding' but raise concerns about the 'somewhat arbitrary age cut-off point of 65 years' and suggest that 'in truncating the age-range of participants, the authors may conceal important hormonally-driven transitions in cognitive function.' They also question whether the linear relationship with age (reviewer comment 5) is appropriate given known non-linear patterns of memory decline in AD.

result: The effect of FH on PAL performance was modified by sex, with men showing greater reductions in cognition compared to women (except in the 6th decade), as demonstrated by the significant Sex x FH interaction.
evaluation: Reviewers explicitly state this finding 'appeared to be particularly pronounced in men' and describe it as part of the 'most significant finding.' No concerns were raised about this sex-specific effect, indicating reviewer acceptance of this result.

result: Women performed better than men on PAL across the lifespan, with the disparity markedly growing around the 5th decade of life (50-70 years old), representing the first demonstration of this sex effect across the entire adult lifespan in a large cohort using the same test.
evaluation: Reviewers find the 'discussion of sex-differences around the 5th decade in relation to menopause and modulating effects of estrogen particularly interesting' but express concern that the age 65 cutoff may 'conceal important hormonally-driven transitions in cognitive function in women.' They request additional analysis to 'look at these factors earlier in the lifespan' and examine 'sharp declines in PAL performance...from the 6th decade onwards.'

result: Educational attainment modified the effect of FH on PAL performance, with FH associated with lower PAL scores at all education levels, but the magnitude of decline was greater at lower educational attainment compared to higher levels.
evaluation: Reviewers do not raise concerns about this finding. However, they do note that 'socioeconomic status (SES) was not explored' and state this is 'not a trivial omission' as educational attainment and other factors 'may all relate to, or interact with, lower SES,' suggesting the interpretation may be incomplete.

result: Diabetes modified the effect of FH on PAL performance, with FH+ participants who also had diabetes showing lower PAL scores compared to FH+ participants without diabetes.
evaluation: Reviewers note that 'the potential role of other risk factors/disease does not appear to have been taken into account' and request clarification or acknowledgment as a limitation. This suggests uncertainty about whether the diabetes effect is adequately isolated from other confounding health factors.

result: In FH+ individuals, the APOE ε4 allele was associated with lower PAL scores in a dose-dependent manner, with each ε4 allele associated with approximately 1.3 word pairs lower performance, and ε4-ε4 homozygotes showing 5 word pairs lower scores compared to ε2-ε3 carriers.
evaluation: Reviewers explicitly note 'the inclusion of APOE genotype data in a large subgroup is a further strength of the study' without raising concerns about these findings, indicating acceptance of this genetic modifier result.

result: Age was significantly associated with PAL performance, with a decline of approximately two word-pairs per decade of life across the 18-85 year age range.
evaluation: Reviewers explicitly question this finding, stating 'The result that PAL performance was linearly associated with participant's age (Figure 2) seems not to be in agreement with findings of memory decline across age which is not described by linear functions but a sinuous curve (cf. Jack et al. on dynamics in AD development).' They request the authors 'comment on this discrepancy.'

result: Educational attainment was a significant predictor of PAL scores, with each milestone of education associated with approximately one-third to one word-pair higher performance, and women showing higher education-related benefits than men at most levels.
evaluation: While reviewers do not directly challenge this finding, they raise a critical concern that 'socioeconomic status (SES) was not explored' and note that 'educational attainment...may all relate to, or interact with, lower SES,' suggesting this result may be confounded by unmeasured SES effects.

result: The MindCrowd study successfully recruited 59,571 qualified participants with diverse demographic characteristics including 62.46% female, 92.03% White, varying educational levels, and 22.76% with family history of AD.
evaluation: Reviewers describe 'The sample size of ~60,000 people is impressive, and permits a well-powered exploration of factors' without raising concerns about the cohort composition itself, though they do note concerns about selection bias and self-report reliability.

result: The study only assessed first-degree family history, potentially including individuals with extended family AD risk in the non-FH group, and did not distinguish between late-onset versus early-onset AD in relatives, which may encode different levels of FH risk.
evaluation: Reviewers directly address this limitation, asking 'was FH related to all members in the family or not? Was FH defined in terms of both sporadic and familial AD?' and requesting clarification about 'age of onset, specific symptom profiles, whether there was functional decline (i.e., differentiating between aMCI and AD).'

result: Sensitivity analyses demonstrated that the FH effect on PAL remains statistically significant even with substantial additional self-report error (up to 24% error still shows significance in >50% of iterations), suggesting self-report error is unlikely to be driving the FH effect.
evaluation: Reviewers express concern that 'the validity and reliability of these data are not presented' and request 'further details regarding how the questions were phrased and how they were coded.' While the sensitivity analysis addresses error rates, reviewers' concerns about the fundamental reliability of self-reported FH remain unaddressed.

result: The cross-sectional study design limits the ability to make determinations about trajectories of change in performance over time within individual subjects, requiring future longitudinal studies.
evaluation: Reviewers do not explicitly comment on this limitation, but it is a standard methodological constraint that is appropriately acknowledged by the authors.

result: Older FH+ participants who consented to the study may represent those who have remained cognitively intact, as participants experiencing noticeable cognitive impairment may choose not to participate, potentially contributing to selection bias.
evaluation: Reviewers note that 'SES may relate to selection bias of individuals who volunteer to take part in such studies,' acknowledging this as a legitimate concern, though they do not specifically address the age-related selection bias hypothesis.

result: This work demonstrates the utility of web-based cohort recruitment, facilitating large sample sizes in a cost- and time-effective fashion, with advantages of larger samples and enriched diversity mostly diminishing potential disadvantages.
evaluation: While reviewers acknowledge the 'impressive' sample size, they raise substantial concerns about 'the validity and reliability of these data' from self-report, request details about 'how the questions were phrased and how they were coded,' and question 'the reliability of these questions' across cultures/languages, suggesting the advantages may not fully overcome the disadvantages.
